The breeder (Hyperion) is a compact D–T spherical tokamak sized to a supply requirement rather than an electrical rating. It runs at scientific gain Q_sci 3.076, producing 85.0 MW of fusion power at 9.66 MA of plasma current. The value it delivers is the neutron economy that gain creates, not electricity sent to a grid.

Every D–T fusion reaction releases one 14.1 MeV neutron. Those neutrons do three jobs. They breed tritium in a lithium-bearing blanket toward a ~4 kg/yr class output. That tritium beta-decays to helium-3 with a 12.3-year half-life, yielding a coproduct near 1.97 kg/yr. And the fast-neutron flux itself is a product: a fusion-representative 14 MeV irradiation source for materials qualification and activation services.
Why the products matter more than the power

Tritium is the base fuel of every D–T fusion program and has no natural terrestrial reservoir at scale. Helium-3 is a strategic material for quantum-computing dilution refrigeration and neutron detection. A true 14 MeV source has no operating equivalent for testing fusion materials. Hyperion is designed to supply all three.

The three products depend on breeding physics that is not yet closed. The tritium breeding ratio (TBR) is treated as a design lever at 1.1 / 1.5 / 1.8, and the reconciliation between an idealized local TBR and the as-built net TBR is an open question at the 1.8 target. Tritium self-sufficiency is not yet proven. These are stated plainly on the pages that follow.
This page describes a design-and-simulation study, not a built machine. Construction begins Q2 2027; first-of-a-kind (FOAK) first tritium is targeted near 2030. No net-gain claim is made before FOAK.

title: The Three Products
lede: Tritium (~4 kg/yr class), helium-3 (~1.97 kg/yr from tritium decay), and 14 MeV neutrons — one machine, three strategic outputs.

Hyperion's three products all trace back to a single physical fact: D–T fusion emits a 14.1 MeV neutron per reaction. At 85.0 MW of fusion power the source term is large, and the machine is engineered to convert that neutron budget into material outputs.

Bred in a lithium-6-bearing blanket via ⁶Li(n,α)T, with neutron multiplication from beryllium or lead. Target output is a ~4 kg/yr class. Tritium is the primary product and the reason the machine is called a breeder.

Not fused directly; it accumulates as tritium beta-decays (³H → ³He, half-life 12.3 yr). About 5.47% of a stored tritium inventory converts per year, giving a coproduct near 1.97 kg/yr under the reference inventory model.

The uncollided fast-neutron flux is offered as an irradiation service. A fusion-representative 14 MeV spectrum is the correct environment for qualifying structural materials, and no fission reactor reproduces it.
Tritium — fusion fuel and neutron-target feedstock
Helium-3 — quantum dilution refrigeration, neutron detection

Tritium and neutron flux are produced in real time while the plasma runs; helium-3 is produced on the slow clock of the 12.3-year tritium decay half-life, accumulating in storage whether or not the machine is running. The foundry therefore has a fast product loop and a slow one, and the two are coupled because helium-3 grows from the tritium the machine chooses to hold.

All three streams are contingent on the same physics. The tritium and helium-3 figures depend on the net tritium breeding ratio clearing self-sufficiency at the 1.8 target — an open reconciliation — and the neutron-service capacity depends on how the fixed neutron budget is allocated between breeding and irradiation. The figures are honest design targets, not demonstrated yields.
This page describes a design-and-simulation study, not a built machine. Construction begins Q2 2027; first-of-a-kind (FOAK) first tritium is targeted near 2030. No net-gain claim is made before FOAK.

title: Tritium: the Primary Product
lede: Tritium is Hyperion's headline output — bred in the blanket toward a ~4 kg/yr class — and the fuel every D–T fusion program depends on.
body: <svg viewBox="0 0 560 300" width="100%" style="max-width:560px;height:auto;display:block;margin:14px 0;font-family:var(--sans,sans-serif)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="20" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="85.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">14 MeV n</text><text x="85.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">from plasma</text><line x1="150" y1="150" x2="210" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="210" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="275.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">⁶Li blanket</text><text x="275.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">(n,α)T</text><line x1="340" y1="150" x2="400" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="400" y="120" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="470.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Tritium</text><text x="470.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">~4 kg/yr</text></svg>

Tritium (³H) is a hydrogen isotope with a 12.3-year half-life. It does not exist in useful natural quantities; today it is produced in small amounts as a by-product of fission reactors. Every deuterium–tritium fusion machine must be supplied with it, and at fleet scale demand outstrips any existing source.

Hyperion breeds its own tritium in a blanket surrounding the plasma. The reaction ⁶Li(n,α)³H captures a neutron on lithium-6 to make one tritium atom plus helium-4, releasing 4.8 MeV. Because the D–T reaction that produced the neutron also consumed one tritium atom, breeding more than one tritium per fusion neutron is what makes the fuel cycle self-sustaining.

At 85.0 MW of D–T fusion power the neutron production rate sets an upper bound on breeding. The reference design targets a tritium output in the ~4 kg/yr class, sized to seed the burner fuel cycle and to supply external offtake. The realized figure depends directly on the tritium breeding ratio achieved.

A target output assumes the net (as-built) TBR clears self-sufficiency with margin. At the 1.8 design target the local-vs-net reconciliation is unresolved, and tritium self-sufficiency is not yet demonstrated in hardware. The ~4 kg/yr class is a design figure, contingent on closing that gate.
This page describes a design-and-simulation study, not a built machine. Construction begins Q2 2027; first-of-a-kind (FOAK) first tritium is targeted near 2030. No net-gain claim is made before FOAK.

title: The ~4 kg/yr Tritium Class
lede: Hyperion's tritium output is quoted as a class near 4 kg/yr — a design figure set by the neutron budget and the achieved breeding ratio.

Tritium output is not a free parameter. It is bounded by how many 14 MeV neutrons the plasma produces and by how efficiently the blanket converts them to bred tritium. At 85.0 MW of fusion power the D–T neutron rate is fixed by physics; the conversion is the tritium breeding ratio (TBR).

The net tritium available for products equals what is bred, minus what the D–T plasma itself burns, minus decay and process losses. Because the plasma consumes tritium to run, only breeding above unity leaves a surplus. The ~4 kg/yr class describes the surplus target under the favorable breeding scenario.

Kronos states this as a class rather than a single guaranteed value because the realized output slides with the TBR lever (1.1 / 1.5 / 1.8), with lithium-6 enrichment, blanket coverage, and tritium holdup. Higher TBR and coverage push output up; ports, structure, and losses pull it down.
Fusion power 85.0 MW → neutron source rate (fixed)
× net TBR → tritium bred per unit time
− plasma burnup − decay − holdup → net surplus
The figure is honest only if the net TBR and self-sufficiency gates close. Both are open at the 1.8 target and are treated as design-and-simulation findings, not demonstrated results.
This page describes a design-and-simulation study, not a built machine. Construction begins Q2 2027; first-of-a-kind (FOAK) first tritium is targeted near 2030. No net-gain claim is made before FOAK.

title: Tritium Decay to Helium-3
lede: Tritium beta-decays to helium-3 with a 12.3-year half-life; this decay, not fusion, is how Hyperion produces its helium-3 coproduct.
body: The decay that makes a second product

<svg viewBox="0 0 480 260" width="100%" style="max-width:480px;height:auto;display:block;margin:14px 0;font-family:var(--sans,sans-serif)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="30" y="120" width="150" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="105.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Tritium (³H)</text><text x="105.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">half-life 12.3 yr</text><line x1="180" y1="150" x2="300" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="240.0" y="144.0" fill="currentColor" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">β⁻ decay</text><text x="240" y="178" fill="currentColor" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">e⁻ + ν̄</text><rect x="300" y="120" width="150" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="375.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Helium-3 (³He)</text><text x="375.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">stable</text><text x="240" y="60" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">³H → ³He + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ   (E_β,max ≈ 18.6 keV)</text><text x="240" y="235" fill="currentColor" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">≈ 5.47% of a T inventory converts to ³He per year</text></svg>

Tritium is radioactive. It undergoes beta-minus decay to helium-3: ³H → ³He + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ, with a half-life of 12.3 years and a maximum beta energy of about 18.6 keV. The emitted electron is low-energy and stopped by millimeters of material, but the daughter nucleus, helium-3, is stable and valuable.

This means any tritium inventory continuously generates helium-3. The conversion rate follows the decay constant λ = ln2 / 12.3 yr, so roughly 5.47% of a stored tritium mass becomes helium-3 each year. Helium-3 that accumulates in storage vessels and getters is periodically extracted and purified.
Why decay is the only terrestrial route

Helium-3 is not fused in the breeder and is not mined on Earth in useful quantity. Tritium decay is effectively the sole terrestrial production path, which is why national helium-3 supplies historically came from decaying nuclear-weapons tritium stockpiles. A tritium-breeding foundry is, by construction, also a helium-3 source.

Because helium-3 grows from the tritium in hand, its production rate is tied to how much tritium is stored and for how long. Inventory strategy — how much tritium is held versus shipped or burned — directly sets the ~1.97 kg/yr helium-3 coproduct figure.
This page describes a design-and-simulation study, not a built machine. Construction begins Q2 2027; first-of-a-kind (FOAK) first tritium is targeted near 2030. No net-gain claim is made before FOAK.

title: The Helium-3 Coproduct
lede: Helium-3 accumulates from tritium decay at roughly 1.97 kg/yr — a strategic material Hyperion produces without any dedicated fusion reaction.
body: <svg viewBox="0 0 480 260" width="100%" style="max-width:480px;height:auto;display:block;margin:14px 0;font-family:var(--sans,sans-serif)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="30" y="120" width="150" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="105.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Tritium (³H)</text><text x="105.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">half-life 12.3 yr</text><line x1="180" y1="150" x2="300" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="240.0" y="144.0" fill="currentColor" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">β⁻ decay</text><text x="240" y="178" fill="currentColor" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">e⁻ + ν̄</text><rect x="300" y="120" width="150" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="375.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Helium-3 (³He)</text><text x="375.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">stable</text><text x="240" y="60" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">³H → ³He + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ   (E_β,max ≈ 18.6 keV)</text><text x="240" y="235" fill="currentColor" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">≈ 5.47% of a T inventory converts to ³He per year</text></svg>

Helium-3 (³He) is the second product of the breeder (Hyperion). It is not created by fusing anything; it appears because the tritium the machine breeds slowly decays. Over the reference inventory and holding times, the coproduct rate is near 1.97 kg/yr.

Helium-3 is scarce and strategically important. Its two largest uses are dilution refrigeration for quantum computing and cryogenics, where a ³He/⁴He mixture reaches millikelvin temperatures, and neutron detection, where ³He proportional counters are a workhorse for security and science. Terrestrial supply is small and has historically depended on decaying weapons tritium.

This number follows from the tritium inventory and the 12.3-year half-life: about 5.47% of the held tritium converts per year. It is therefore a coproduct of the tritium program, coupled to how much tritium Hyperion breeds and stores. More tritium held for longer yields more helium-3; tritium shipped or burned yields less.

Because helium-3 is downstream of bred tritium, it inherits the same honest gate: it depends on the net tritium breeding ratio and self-sufficiency clearing at the 1.8 target. The ~1.97 kg/yr figure is a design-and-simulation estimate, not a demonstrated yield.

title: The ~1.97 kg/yr Helium-3 Figure
lede: The reference helium-3 coproduct rate near 1.97 kg/yr follows directly from the stored tritium mass and the 12.3-year decay constant.
body: <svg viewBox="0 0 560 300" width="100%" style="max-width:560px;height:auto;display:block;margin:14px 0;font-family:var(--sans,sans-serif)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="20" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="85.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Tritium held</text><text x="85.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">inventory</text><line x1="150" y1="150" x2="210" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="210" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="275.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">β⁻ decay</text><text x="275.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">5.47%/yr</text><line x1="340" y1="150" x2="400" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="400" y="120" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="470.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Helium-3</text><text x="470.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">~1.97 kg/yr</text></svg>

The helium-3 production rate is a decay calculation, not a fusion calculation. If a tritium inventory of mass M is held, helium-3 grows at approximately λM per year, where λ = ln2 / 12.3 yr ≈ 0.0563 per year, and the mass-3 daughter carries essentially the same atom count. Over a year this is about 5.47% of the tritium mass converting to helium-3.

Under the reference tritium inventory and holding assumptions consistent with the ~4 kg/yr class breeding target, the resulting coproduct rate is near 1.97 kg/yr. The figure is deliberately quoted to three figures because it is a computed consequence of the inventory model, but it is only as firm as that model and the breeding it assumes.
Higher standing tritium inventory → more He-3 per year
Shorter tritium residence (shipped/burned sooner) → less He-3
Extraction cadence and getter efficiency set recoverable fraction
Any shortfall in net TBR reduces both tritium and He-3 together

1.97 kg/yr is a design-and-simulation estimate contingent on the tritium program meeting its targets. It is a coproduct: Hyperion is optimized to breed tritium, and helium-3 is the yield of holding that tritium over time.

Deuterium–tritium fusion releases 17.6 MeV per reaction, split as a 3.5 MeV helium-4 (alpha) that stays magnetically confined and heats the plasma, and a 14.1 MeV neutron that escapes it. The neutron carries about 80% of the energy and, being uncharged, leaves the magnetic field and enters the surrounding structures. That escaping neutron is Hyperion's working currency.

At 85.0 MW of fusion power the neutron production rate is large and monoenergetic at birth near 14.1 MeV. This is a distinctive spectrum: fission reactors peak around 1–2 MeV, and no fission source reproduces the 14 MeV fusion peak that governs displacement damage and (n,2n), (n,α), and (n,p) reactions in fusion materials.
Breed tritium via ⁶Li(n,α)T in the blanket
Drive activation and transmutation for isotope services
Provide a fusion-representative irradiation environment for materials

There is exactly one neutron per fusion event, so the products compete for the same budget. Neutrons captured for breeding are not available for external irradiation, and blanket coverage designed to maximize TBR limits open test volume. Product planning is fundamentally the allocation of a fixed neutron budget.

D–T fusion emits exactly one neutron per reaction. At 85.0 MW the total neutron production rate is set by physics and cannot be increased without more fusion power. Every function the breeder performs draws from this one budget, so the design is an allocation problem.
Breeding: neutrons captured on ⁶Li to make tritium (the largest claim)
Multiplication: (n,2n) on beryllium or lead adds neutrons before capture
Losses: absorption in structure, coolant, and ports (unproductive)
Streaming: neutrons escaping through gaps and penetrations
Services: flux deliberately routed to irradiation and activation stations

Because the plasma burns one tritium per neutron, raw breeding at one-for-one cannot be self-sufficient once losses are counted. Neutron multipliers such as beryllium — ⁹Be(n,2n) — or lead increase the neutron count before capture, which is how a design pushes net TBR above 1.0 with margin. Multiplier choice, thickness, and enrichment are the main levers.

A useful mental model: source neutrons plus multiplier gain must exceed breeding capture plus parasitic losses plus streaming, with the surplus setting how much flux can be sold as irradiation service. This balance, computed in neutronics simulation, is where the TBR lever and the honest local-vs-net reconciliation live.

First wall: neutrons pass through a hafnium-carbide-protected wall
Multiplier: (n,2n) on Be/Pb raises the neutron count
Breeder: ⁶Li(n,α)T captures neutrons to make tritium

Tritium and neutron flux are produced in real time while the plasma runs. Helium-3 is produced on a slow clock set by the 12.3-year decay half-life, so it accumulates in storage regardless of whether the machine is running. The foundry therefore has a fast product loop and a slow one.

The breeder and extraction steps are where the open questions live: whether net TBR clears self-sufficiency with margin, and how much tritium is lost to holdup. The flow is a design-and-simulation description until FOAK demonstrates it.

title: The Tritium Breeding Ratio Design Lever
lede: TBR — tritium atoms bred per fusion neutron — is treated as a design lever at 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8, spanning thin margin to the reference target.

The tritium breeding ratio (TBR) is the number of tritium atoms bred in the blanket per fusion neutron produced by the plasma. Because the D–T reaction consumes one tritium per neutron, a TBR above 1.0 is the condition for the fuel cycle to sustain itself and produce a surplus.

Kronos does not quote a single TBR. It treats TBR as a design lever studied at three points — 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8 — because the achievable value depends on choices still under study: lithium-6 enrichment, neutron multiplier type and thickness, blanket coverage fraction, and structural material selection.
TBR 1.1 — barely above breakeven; thin margin, minimal surplus, fragile to losses
TBR 1.5 — a comfortable working point with real surplus for offtake and startup of new units
TBR 1.8 — the reference target that supports the ~4 kg/yr class and fleet doubling

A design TBR above 1.0 does not guarantee self-sufficiency, because the quoted value is often the local ratio in an idealized blanket cell. The as-built net TBR is lower once ports, gaps, structure, and coolant are included. The margin between the two is the crux of the honest reconciliation.

title: TBR 1.1: the Thin-Margin Point
lede: At TBR 1.1 the blanket breeds barely more tritium than the plasma burns — self-sufficient in principle, but fragile to any real-world loss.

TBR 1.1 means eleven tritium atoms bred for every ten fusion neutrons — a 10% surplus over the one-for-one the plasma burns. On paper this clears self-sufficiency. In practice it leaves almost no room for the losses that every real blanket incurs.

The concern is that the 10% headroom is smaller than the typical penalty from ports, gaps, structural absorption, coolant, and tritium holdup. A local TBR of 1.1 can become a net TBR below 1.0 once those are counted, at which point the machine consumes more tritium than it makes and cannot sustain its own fuel.

TBR 1.1 is a meaningful design point for studying the lower bound: it defines the minimum breeding performance the blanket must exceed and stresses the loss budget. It is not the target for a foundry expected to supply external offtake or seed new units, because it leaves essentially no surplus for either.
The lesson of the low point
Self-sufficiency requires margin, not merely TBR > 1.0
At 1.1, holdup and streaming can erase the surplus
Offtake and fleet growth need a higher working point
1.1 is therefore studied as a floor to design against, not as the operating goal. The reference target is higher precisely so that net TBR survives the reconciliation.

title: TBR 1.5: the Working Point
lede: At TBR 1.5 the blanket breeds a 50% surplus over plasma burn — enough margin to absorb real losses and still deliver offtake.

TBR 1.5 breeds fifteen tritium atoms per ten fusion neutrons. The 50% surplus is large enough that even after ports, structural absorption, coolant, streaming, and holdup are subtracted, a net TBR comfortably above 1.0 can remain. That surviving margin is what becomes shippable tritium and startup inventory for new units.

This point is attractive because it is a plausible working target: reachable with moderate lithium-6 enrichment and a beryllium or lead multiplier, without pushing coverage to impractical fractions. It balances breeding performance against the need to keep penetrations for heating, diagnostics, and maintenance.
Net self-sufficiency with a real safety margin
Startup inventory to fuel the next unit (fleet doubling)
Robustness to blanket degradation and outages

1.5 is a neutronics result under specific blanket assumptions, not a measured quantity. The as-built net value depends on the final coverage fraction and loss budget, which is why the reconciliation between local and net TBR remains the governing open question even at this favorable point. A local 1.5 that erodes to a net figure near breakeven would still fail the surplus mission, so the margin at 1.5 is best read as a buffer against the reconciliation penalty rather than a guaranteed surplus.
This page describes a design-and-simulation study, not a built machine. Construction begins Q2 2027; first-of-a-kind (FOAK) first tritium is targeted near 2030. No net-gain claim is made before FOAK.

title: TBR 1.8: the Reference Target
lede: TBR 1.8 is Hyperion's reference target — the breeding performance behind the ~4 kg/yr class — and the point where the local-vs-net reconciliation is open.
body: The target that sets the product figures

TBR 1.8 breeds eighteen tritium atoms per ten fusion neutrons, an 80% surplus. It is the reference target because it is the breeding level consistent with the ~4 kg/yr tritium class, the ~1.97 kg/yr helium-3 coproduct, and enough surplus to seed additional units on a useful timescale.

Reaching 1.8 requires favorable choices across the board: high lithium-6 enrichment, an effective neutron multiplier, and high blanket coverage. Those same choices compete with the practical need for ports and penetrations, which is exactly why 1.8 is a target rather than a settled result.

This is the crux flagged plainly in Hyperion's open-questions record. A local TBR of 1.8 computed for an idealized, fully covered blanket cell is not the same as the net TBR of the real machine with its access ports, structural gaps, coolant channels, and tritium holdup. Whether realistic blanket coverage and losses leave net TBR high enough to hit the product targets is not yet resolved.
Net (as-built) TBR: lower by an amount still being quantified
Gate: net must stay ≥ 1.0 with margin AND support ~4 kg/yr surplus
Kronos states this as an unresolved design-and-simulation question. The product figures are contingent on closing it; no self-sufficiency claim is made in hardware before FOAK.

Neutronics simulations often report a local tritium breeding ratio: the breeding computed for an idealized blanket module, fully surrounding the plasma, with no penetrations and simplified structure. That number can reach the 1.8 target. It is not the number that governs the fuel cycle.
The governing quantity is the net TBR of the complete machine, which is lower because real neutrons are lost to effects the ideal cell ignores:
Ports and penetrations for heating, fueling, diagnostics, and pumping
Gaps between blanket modules and around the center post
Parasitic absorption in structural steel, welds, and manifolds
Absorption and moderation in coolant and tritium-carrier fluids
Streaming of neutrons out through open lines of sight
Why it is flagged as open

The reconciliation is listed among Hyperion's principal open questions because the magnitude of the penalty — how far net falls below local — is exactly what determines whether the machine is self-sufficient with margin. At the 1.8 target this has not been closed to Kronos's own standard. Reporting a local figure as if it were net would overstate the design, and Kronos declines to do that.

Closure requires full-geometry neutronics with realistic ports and structure, blanket coverage accounting, and eventually measured tritium production at FOAK. Until then, net TBR and the product targets that depend on it are stated as contingent design-and-simulation values.

Tritium self-sufficiency means the machine breeds at least as much tritium as it burns, plus enough to cover losses and, for a foundry, to ship and to seed new units. It is the precondition for a D–T fusion economy, because there is no external tritium supply at fleet scale.

Hyperion is designed toward self-sufficiency, but Kronos does not claim it is achieved. It is a design-and-simulation objective gated on the net TBR clearing 1.0 with margin — and the local-vs-net reconciliation at the 1.8 target is unresolved. No hardware demonstration exists before FOAK first tritium near 2030.
Self-sufficiency is not just net TBR > 1.0. The realistic condition accounts for:
Plasma burnup — tritium the reaction consumes (only a few percent is burned per pass; the rest is recycled)
Radioactive decay — 5.47% of held inventory per year lost to He-3
Holdup — tritium trapped in walls, blanket, and pumps
Processing losses — inefficiency in extraction and purification
Startup inventory — tritium needed before the machine breeds its own

Overstating self-sufficiency is the most common way fusion breeding claims fail scrutiny. By treating TBR as a lever, separating local from net, and naming self-sufficiency as unproven, Kronos keeps the product figures honest: the ~4 kg/yr class and ~1.97 kg/yr helium-3 are targets contingent on this gate closing.

title: Blanket Coverage and TBR
lede: TBR scales with how completely the blanket surrounds the plasma; ports and the center post open gaps that lower net breeding.
body: <svg viewBox="0 0 560 300" width="100%" style="max-width:560px;height:auto;display:block;margin:14px 0;font-family:var(--sans,sans-serif)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="150" y="40" width="26" height="220" rx="4" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="163" y="275" fill="currentColor" font-size="9" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">center post</text><path d="M185,60 C300,70 320,130 300,150 C320,170 300,230 185,240 C230,200 230,100 185,60 Z" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2"/><text x="255" y="155" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600">D–T plasma</text><text x="255" y="172" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">δ = −0.30</text><path d="M180,45 C330,55 360,145 335,150 C360,155 330,255 180,258" fill="none" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="10" opacity="0.85"/><text x="350" y="100" fill="currentColor" font-size="10" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">blanket</text><line x1="365" y1="150" x2="470" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="417.5" y="144.0" fill="currentColor" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">products</text><rect x="470" y="60" width="80" height="40" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="510.0" y="84.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">T</text><rect x="470" y="130" width="80" height="40" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="510.0" y="154.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">He-3</text><rect x="470" y="200" width="80" height="40" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="510.0" y="224.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="10" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">14 MeV n</text></svg>

The tritium breeding ratio depends strongly on solid-angle coverage: the fraction of neutrons that actually reach breeding material before being lost. A blanket that surrounds more of the plasma captures more neutrons and breeds more tritium. Any area that is not blanket — a port, a gap, the inboard center post — is area that does not breed.

Spherical tokamaks make this trade sharper. The compact center post that carries the toroidal-field conductors occupies inboard space, and shielding it from neutron damage competes with breeding there. So inboard coverage, which matters a great deal for TBR, is constrained by the machine's geometry.
Gaps between blanket modules for assembly and maintenance

Coverage is precisely why local TBR overstates net TBR. A cell calculation assumes full coverage; the real machine cannot. Recovering breeding lost to ports — by breeding in more locations, minimizing gaps, and adding neutron multiplication near penetrations — is central to closing the net-TBR gate at the 1.8 target.
Coverage is a design-and-simulation trade under active study; the achievable net TBR follows from where it settles.

title: Lithium-6 Enrichment and Breeding
lede: Tritium is bred on lithium-6; enriching the lithium in ⁶Li raises capture and is one of the strongest levers on TBR.
body: <svg viewBox="0 0 560 300" width="100%" style="max-width:560px;height:auto;display:block;margin:14px 0;font-family:var(--sans,sans-serif)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="20" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="85.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">14 MeV n</text><text x="85.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">from plasma</text><line x1="150" y1="150" x2="210" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="210" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="275.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">⁶Li</text><text x="275.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">(n,α)T + 4.8 MeV</text><line x1="340" y1="150" x2="400" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="400" y="120" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="470.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Tritium</text><text x="470.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">+ ⁴He</text></svg>

Tritium breeding in the blanket runs on two reactions with lithium. The dominant one at low energy is ⁶Li(n,α)³H, which captures a neutron on lithium-6 to produce tritium and helium-4, releasing 4.8 MeV of useful heat. A second channel, ⁷Li(n,n'α)³H, breeds on lithium-7 but only for fast neutrons and consumes energy.

Natural lithium is only about 7.6% lithium-6, the rest being lithium-7. Because ⁶Li is the workhorse breeder, enriching the lithium in lithium-6 raises the breeding cross-section available and is one of the most direct ways to increase TBR. Reference blanket studies assume enrichment well above natural abundance.
Higher ⁶Li fraction → higher breeding, higher TBR
Enrichment is a supply-chain and process undertaking
Over-enrichment past a point yields diminishing returns as the blanket becomes optically thick
⁷Li still contributes fast breeding and neutron economy

Lithium-6 is itself a controlled, limited material, and enriched-lithium supply is part of the breeder's feedstock planning. It is a real engineering and sourcing constraint, treated here as a physics-and-process design factor. It carries no economics on this page by policy — only its role as a TBR lever.

title: Neutron Multiplication in the Blanket
lede: One neutron per fusion cannot self-breed after losses; (n,2n) multipliers like beryllium or lead add neutrons before capture to lift net TBR.
body: Why you need more than one neutron

<svg viewBox="0 0 560 300" width="100%" style="max-width:560px;height:auto;display:block;margin:14px 0;font-family:var(--sans,sans-serif)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="20" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="85.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">1 fusion n</text><text x="85.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">14.1 MeV</text><line x1="150" y1="150" x2="210" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="210" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="275.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Multiplier</text><text x="275.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">(n,2n): Be/Pb</text><line x1="340" y1="150" x2="400" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="400" y="120" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="470.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">>1 n</text><text x="470.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">then bred</text></svg>

D–T fusion gives exactly one neutron per reaction, and the plasma burns one tritium per reaction. So even a perfect blanket that bred one tritium per neutron would only break even before any losses. Once ports, structure, and holdup subtract from the budget, one-for-one breeding falls below self-sufficiency.

The fix is neutron multiplication: reactions that turn one incoming neutron into two. The two standard multipliers are beryllium, via ⁹Be(n,2n), and lead, via ²⁰⁸Pb(n,2n). Placed ahead of or within the breeding zone, a multiplier increases the neutron population before capture on lithium-6, which is how a design lifts net TBR above 1.0 with margin.
Beryllium: strong multiplier, but a limited and safety-sensitive material
Lead: multiplies and also acts as coolant/carrier in some blanket concepts
Multiplier thickness and placement tune the neutron economy
Multiplication competes with parasitic absorption for the same neutrons

Multiplication is the primary tool for recovering breeding lost to real-machine effects, so it is central to closing the local-vs-net TBR gap at the 1.8 target. The achievable gain is a neutronics result under study, not a demonstrated value, and it depends on the final blanket geometry and materials.

title: Tritium Burnup Fraction
lede: The plasma burns only a small fraction of the tritium fed to it per pass; the rest is pumped, cleaned, and recycled — which shapes the fuel loop.
body: Most tritium is recycled, not burned

<svg viewBox="0 0 560 300" width="100%" style="max-width:560px;height:auto;display:block;margin:14px 0;font-family:var(--sans,sans-serif)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="20" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="85.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Tritium fed</text><text x="85.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">fueling</text><line x1="150" y1="150" x2="210" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="210" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="275.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Plasma</text><text x="275.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">few % burned</text><line x1="340" y1="150" x2="400" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="400" y="120" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="470.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Exhaust</text><text x="470.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">recycle</text></svg>

A common misconception is that all tritium injected into the plasma fuses. It does not. Only a few percent of the tritium fed to the plasma actually reacts on a single pass; the large majority is exhausted unburned, pumped out of the vessel, separated from helium ash and impurities, and re-injected.

This low single-pass burnup fraction has two consequences for what Hyperion makes. First, the fuel-processing plant must handle a tritium throughput far larger than the net amount burned, which drives the size and speed of the tritium plant. Second, tritium spends time in walls, pumps, and processing lines — holdup — where some is lost to decay and permeation.

Net tritium balance is what is bred minus what is burned minus what is lost. Because burnup per pass is small, the dominant tritium consumer is not the fusion reaction directly but the accumulated inventory locked in the loop and lost to decay and holdup over time. Breeding must cover all of it.
Large recycled throughput sizes the tritium plant
Holdup in the loop is tritium unavailable for offtake
Fast, efficient recycling reduces standing inventory and loss
Burnup and breeding together set the net surplus
This page describes a design-and-simulation study, not a built machine. Construction begins Q2 2027; first-of-a-kind (FOAK) first tritium is targeted near 2030. No net-gain claim is made before FOAK.

Net product is always less than gross breeding. Between the neutron captured on lithium-6 and the tritium loaded into a shipping container, several loss mechanisms act, and each one is subtracted from the surplus that the ~4 kg/yr class and the helium-3 coproduct depend on.
Radioactive decay: ~5.47% of held tritium per year becomes He-3 (recovered as coproduct, but lost as tritium)
Permeation: tritium diffuses through hot metal walls and must be contained and recaptured
Holdup: tritium trapped in blanket material, first wall, pumps, and getters
Processing inefficiency: incomplete extraction and purification
Streaming and leakage losses in the vacuum and fuel systems

Holdup is particularly important for a foundry because tritium sitting in the machine is tritium that is neither shipped nor available to burn, and it steadily decays. Minimizing standing inventory and residence time keeps more of the bred tritium available as product.

The loss budget is what separates a promising local TBR from a self-sufficient net TBR with saleable surplus. A machine can breed above 1.0 locally and still fail to ship product if holdup and losses are large. Quantifying and bounding these losses is part of the open self-sufficiency question, verified by measured inventory at FOAK.

title: Startup Tritium Inventory
lede: A breeder cannot breed before it runs, so the first machine needs an external tritium charge to start — the startup inventory problem.
body: <svg viewBox="0 0 560 300" width="100%" style="max-width:560px;height:auto;display:block;margin:14px 0;font-family:var(--sans,sans-serif)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="20" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="85.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">External T</text><text x="85.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">startup charge</text><line x1="150" y1="150" x2="210" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="210" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="275.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Hyperion</text><text x="275.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">runs & breeds</text><line x1="340" y1="150" x2="400" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="400" y="120" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="470.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Surplus T</text><text x="470.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">seeds next unit</text></svg>

Tritium breeding requires a running D–T plasma, but running a D–T plasma requires tritium. The first unit therefore needs a startup inventory of tritium sourced externally before it can breed its own. This is the startup inventory problem, and it is a real constraint on how a fusion fleet can grow.

Today external tritium comes from fission reactors in limited quantity. FOAK Hyperion is expected to draw on such supply to begin operation near 2030, then transition toward breeding its own fuel. Whether it can also breed enough surplus to charge the next unit is set by the net TBR.
Why net TBR governs fleet growth

Once a machine is self-sufficient, only the surplus above self-sufficiency is available to start additional units. A net TBR of 1.1 leaves almost none; 1.5 and 1.8 leave progressively more. The higher the net TBR, the faster a fleet can double, because each machine can seed the next sooner. This is the doubling-time argument for targeting 1.8.
Self-sufficiency lets a unit sustain itself
Surplus above self-sufficiency seeds new units
Net TBR sets how quickly the fleet can grow
The startup charge and the surplus economy are design-and-simulation planning, contingent on the self-sufficiency gate.

title: Doubling Time and Fleet Growth
lede: Doubling time — how long a breeder takes to make enough surplus tritium to start another — falls as net TBR rises, linking breeding to fleet scale.
body: <svg viewBox="0 0 560 270" width="100%" style="max-width:560px;height:auto;display:block;margin:14px 0;font-family:var(--sans,sans-serif)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="90" y="141.0" width="90" height="99.00000000000001" rx="4" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="135" y="133.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600">TBR 1.1</text><text x="135" y="258" fill="currentColor" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">margin-thin</text><rect x="230" y="105.0" width="90" height="135.0" rx="4" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="275" y="97.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600">TBR 1.5</text><text x="275" y="258" fill="currentColor" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">working point</text><rect x="370" y="78.0" width="90" height="162.0" rx="4" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="415" y="70.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600">TBR 1.8</text><text x="415" y="258" fill="currentColor" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">target</text><line x1="40" y1="150" x2="480" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.2" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/><text x="486" y="154" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">TBR = 1.0</text><text x="486" y="168" fill="currentColor" font-size="8.5" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">self-sufficiency floor</text></svg>

Doubling time is the interval over which a breeder produces enough surplus tritium, beyond its own needs, to provide the full startup inventory for an identical new unit. It is a standard measure of how fast a breeding fleet can grow, borrowed from the same logic used for breeder reactors.

The controlling quantity is the net TBR above self-sufficiency. A machine breeding at net 1.1 has almost no surplus and a very long doubling time; a machine at net 1.5 or 1.8 accumulates a startup charge much sooner. Higher breeding and lower losses both shorten it.
Net TBR above 1.0 — the surplus rate
Startup inventory required per new unit
Tritium losses and holdup that erode surplus
Decay of stored surplus while it accumulates

The reference TBR target of 1.8 is chosen partly so that doubling time is short enough for a fleet to grow on a useful schedule — FOAK to NOAK to BOAK and beyond — rather than being throttled by fuel. This is the practical link between the breeding-ratio lever and the foundry's role as the fuel source for the wider program, including the burner's eventual helium-3 pathway.
Doubling time is a design-and-simulation projection contingent on net TBR and self-sufficiency, both of which remain open.

title: Extracting Tritium from the Blanket
lede: Bred tritium must be recovered from the blanket carrier before it can be stored, decayed to helium-3, or shipped — the first step of the product path.
body: From bred atom to recoverable gas

<svg viewBox="0 0 560 300" width="100%" style="max-width:560px;height:auto;display:block;margin:14px 0;font-family:var(--sans,sans-serif)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="20" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="85.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Blanket</text><text x="85.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">bred T in carrier</text><line x1="150" y1="150" x2="210" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="210" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="275.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Extraction</text><text x="275.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">strip & collect</text><line x1="340" y1="150" x2="400" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="400" y="120" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="470.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Purification</text><text x="470.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">product-grade</text></svg>

Tritium is created inside the blanket embedded in whatever carries the breeding material — a solid ceramic pebble bed, a liquid lithium-lead eutectic, or a molten salt, depending on blanket concept. Extraction is the process of getting that tritium out of the carrier and into a gas stream that can be purified and stored.

The method depends on the carrier. Solid breeders release tritium to a purge gas (typically helium with a little hydrogen) that sweeps through the pebble bed at temperature. Liquid metal breeders use permeators, vacuum degassing, or gas contactors to strip tritium from the flowing eutectic. In every case the goal is to remove tritium fast enough to limit holdup and inventory.
Slow extraction increases standing tritium inventory (more decay, more holdup)
Fast extraction reduces loss and frees tritium for offtake sooner
Extraction efficiency directly enters the tritium loss budget
Purge/carrier chemistry must not damage the blanket

Extraction is where net TBR becomes recoverable product. A high breeding ratio is only useful if the tritium can be pulled out efficiently. Extraction efficiency is therefore part of the self-sufficiency calculation and is a design-and-simulation subject until demonstrated at FOAK.

title: Tritium Plant Integration
lede: The tritium plant closes the fuel loop: it separates exhaust, recovers bred tritium, purifies it, and returns fuel — throughput far exceeds burnup.
body: The plant that closes the loop

<svg viewBox="0 0 560 300" width="100%" style="max-width:560px;height:auto;display:block;margin:14px 0;font-family:var(--sans,sans-serif)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="20" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="85.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Exhaust + purge</text><text x="85.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">T, D, He, imps</text><line x1="150" y1="150" x2="210" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="210" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="275.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Isotope sep.</text><text x="275.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">ISS/PERMCAT</text><line x1="340" y1="150" x2="400" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="400" y="120" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="470.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Fuel & product</text><text x="470.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">T + He-3</text></svg>

The tritium plant is the chemical heart of the foundry. It takes two feeds — the plasma exhaust (mostly unburned deuterium and tritium plus helium ash) and the blanket purge or carrier stream (bred tritium) — and turns them into clean fuel for re-injection and product tritium for storage and offtake.
Exhaust processing: remove impurities and helium ash
Blanket tritium recovery: strip tritium from purge/carrier
Storage and delivery: getter beds hold and dispense tritium
Detritiation: recover tritium from waste gas and water streams

Because single-pass burnup is only a few percent, the plant recycles a throughput many times the net tritium consumed. This makes plant speed and reliability, not just breeding, a determinant of how much standing inventory the machine carries.

Product tritium is drawn from the storage subsystem after purification and assay. Helium-3 accumulates from decay within the storage beds and is separated during periodic processing. The plant is therefore the collection point for two of Hyperion's three product streams.
Plant integration is engineered to minimize holdup and loss, both of which enter the self-sufficiency gate. It is a design-and-simulation system until commissioned toward FOAK.

How much tritium the foundry holds at any moment is a managed quantity, not an accident. Standing inventory sits in the fuel loop, the storage getters, the blanket, and in transit. Every gram carries three consequences: it decays to helium-3 at 5.47% per year, it represents a radiological hazard to be contained, and it is capital of the fuel cycle that could otherwise be shipped or burned.
Hold enough tritium to run reliably and cover outages
Minimize standing inventory to limit decay loss and hazard
Hold tritium deliberately when helium-3 coproduct is prioritized
Reserve surplus to seed new units (fleet growth)
Meet offtake commitments for external tritium

These objectives conflict. Holding more tritium produces more helium-3 but loses more tritium to decay and raises the inventory to be safeguarded. Holding less reduces loss and hazard but leaves less buffer and less coproduct. Inventory strategy is where those trades are resolved.
The link to the product figures

The ~1.97 kg/yr helium-3 coproduct figure is, in effect, an inventory-management outcome: it reflects a chosen standing tritium inventory and holding time. Change the inventory policy and the coproduct rate changes with it. Both product figures are therefore coupled through the same managed variable.
Inventory management also feeds accountancy and safeguards, since every gram must be tracked. It is engineered as part of the design-and-simulation program ahead of FOAK.

title: Tritium Storage and Getters
lede: Tritium is stored on metal-hydride getter beds that absorb it as a solid hydride and release it on heating — the safe, dense way to hold the fuel.
body: Holding a gas as a solid

<svg viewBox="0 0 560 300" width="100%" style="max-width:560px;height:auto;display:block;margin:14px 0;font-family:var(--sans,sans-serif)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="20" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="85.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Tritium gas</text><text x="85.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">from plant</text><line x1="150" y1="150" x2="210" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="210" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="275.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Getter bed</text><text x="275.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">metal hydride</text><line x1="340" y1="150" x2="400" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="400" y="120" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="470.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">On-demand</text><text x="470.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">heat → release</text></svg>

Storing tritium as a compressed gas is undesirable: it is a mobile radiological hazard and it permeates hot metal. Instead, tritium is stored on getter beds — metals such as uranium or a titanium/zirconium alloy that absorb hydrogen isotopes chemically, forming a stable metal hydride at room temperature and releasing the gas when heated.

This gives dense, low-pressure storage that is intrinsically safer: at rest the tritium is locked in a solid, and it is liberated only by deliberate heating. Getter beds serve as both the storage reservoir and the metered delivery system that feeds tritium back to fueling on demand.
Low-pressure, solid-bound storage reduces leak and permeation risk
Reversible: absorb when cool, release when hot
Meterable delivery for fueling and for shipping
Compatible with accountancy — bed inventory can be assayed

Because stored tritium decays, helium-3 accumulates within the getter beds over time. Helium-3 is not absorbed by the getter, so it collects as a gas and is periodically pumped off and collected — the storage system is also a helium-3 harvest point. Bed design and cycling therefore influence both product streams and are part of the design-and-simulation program.

title: Tritium Accountancy and Safeguards
lede: Every gram of tritium is tracked by mass balance and assay; accountancy underpins safety, regulatory compliance, and honest product reporting.
body: <svg viewBox="0 0 560 300" width="100%" style="max-width:560px;height:auto;display:block;margin:14px 0;font-family:var(--sans,sans-serif)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="20" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="85.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Bred + received</text><text x="85.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">inputs</text><line x1="150" y1="150" x2="210" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="210" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="275.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Mass balance</text><text x="275.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">assay & track</text><line x1="340" y1="150" x2="400" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="400" y="120" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="470.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Burned/shipped/held</text><text x="470.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">outputs</text></svg>

Tritium is radioactive, mobile, and strategically controlled, so a foundry must account for it precisely. Accountancy is the continuous mass balance of tritium across the whole system: what is bred, what is received as startup charge, what is burned, what decays to helium-3, what is held, and what is shipped.

The balance must close within tight tolerance. A discrepancy between expected and measured inventory — material unaccounted for — is both a safety flag (possible leak or holdup) and a regulatory concern. Assay techniques such as calorimetry (measuring decay heat), gas analysis, and getter-bed inventory measurement establish the actual holdings.
Honest product figures require verified inventory, not estimates
Decay accounting ties the tritium and helium-3 balances together
Holdup shows up as unaccounted material and drives loss reduction
Safeguards and licensing require demonstrable control of the material

Hyperion's licensing pathway treats bred tritium and helium-3 as byproduct material, which places accountancy at the center of compliance. Rigorous tracking is what lets Kronos state product figures as measured quantities once FOAK operates, rather than as projections. Until then, the inventory model is a design-and-simulation construct.

title: Decay Chain and Shelf Life
lede: Tritium's 12.3-year half-life means stored fuel steadily converts to helium-3; the same decay that ages the tritium creates the second product.
body: <svg viewBox="0 0 480 260" width="100%" style="max-width:480px;height:auto;display:block;margin:14px 0;font-family:var(--sans,sans-serif)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="30" y="120" width="150" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="105.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Tritium (³H)</text><text x="105.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">half-life 12.3 yr</text><line x1="180" y1="150" x2="300" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="240.0" y="144.0" fill="currentColor" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">β⁻ decay</text><text x="240" y="178" fill="currentColor" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">e⁻ + ν̄</text><rect x="300" y="120" width="150" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="375.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Helium-3 (³He)</text><text x="375.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">stable</text><text x="240" y="60" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">³H → ³He + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ   (E_β,max ≈ 18.6 keV)</text><text x="240" y="235" fill="currentColor" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">≈ 5.47% of a T inventory converts to ³He per year</text></svg>

Tritium has a half-life of 12.3 years, decaying by beta emission to stable helium-3. This single fact governs both the shelf life of stored tritium and the production of the helium-3 coproduct — they are the same process viewed two ways.

As a shelf-life issue, decay means tritium in storage loses about 5.47% of its mass to helium-3 each year. A batch held for years is measurably depleted, and the helium-3 that forms mixes with the tritium and must be separated before the tritium is used or shipped, because helium-3 is a strong neutron absorber and a fuel contaminant if left in.
Maximum beta energy ≈ 18.6 keV (low, easily shielded)
Turning a liability into a product

Because the decay is unavoidable, the foundry treats the resulting helium-3 as a deliberate coproduct rather than waste. Storage and processing are designed to collect the helium-3 cleanly during the same separation that keeps the tritium pure. The ~1.97 kg/yr helium-3 figure is the harvested result of this shelf-life process across the standing inventory.
The decay chain ends at stable helium-3 — there is no further radioactive daughter, which is part of why the material is attractive and safe to handle.

title: Why Helium-3 Matters
lede: Helium-3 is scarce and strategically important for quantum-computing cryogenics and neutron detection; Hyperion produces it as a decay coproduct.
body: A small market for a rare isotope

<svg viewBox="0 0 560 240" width="100%" style="max-width:560px;height:auto;display:block;margin:14px 0;font-family:var(--sans,sans-serif)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="210" y="20" width="140" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="280.0" y="45.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Hyperion</text><text x="280.0" y="62.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">isotope foundry</text><line x1="280" y1="76" x2="100" y2="146" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="30" y="150" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="100.0" y="177.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="12" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Tritium</text><text x="100.0" y="194.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">fusion fuel · targets</text><line x1="280" y1="76" x2="280" y2="146" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="210" y="150" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="280.0" y="177.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="12" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Helium-3</text><text x="280.0" y="194.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">quantum · detection</text><line x1="280" y1="76" x2="460" y2="146" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="390" y="150" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="460.0" y="177.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="12" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">14 MeV n</text><text x="460.0" y="194.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">materials qual.</text></svg>

Helium-3 is one of the rarest useful isotopes on Earth. It is not mined, not manufactured directly at scale, and effectively produced only by the decay of tritium. Global supply is measured in kilograms per year and has historically depended on drawing down decaying nuclear-weapons tritium stockpiles, a source that is finite and shrinking.
Dilution refrigeration: ³He/⁴He mixtures reach millikelvin temperatures needed for superconducting quantum computers and sensitive detectors
Neutron detection: ³He proportional counters are a standard, high-efficiency detector for security portals, safeguards, and neutron science

The quantum-computing use is the fastest-growing. Every dilution refrigerator that cools a superconducting quantum processor needs a helium-3 charge, and the supply constraint is a recognized bottleneck for scaling quantum hardware.
Why a breeder is a natural source

A tritium-breeding foundry produces helium-3 as an inevitable coproduct of holding tritium. Hyperion's ~1.97 kg/yr coproduct is meaningful against a global supply of only a few kilograms per year. The value here is strategic availability of a scarce enabling material — this page makes only the physical and supply case, with no commercial content.

title: Helium-3 for Quantum Computing
lede: Superconducting quantum computers run at millikelvin temperatures reached with helium-3 dilution refrigeration; He-3 supply constrains the field.
body: The coldest place in the machine

<svg viewBox="0 0 560 300" width="100%" style="max-width:560px;height:auto;display:block;margin:14px 0;font-family:var(--sans,sans-serif)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="20" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="85.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">He-3 charge</text><text x="85.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">dilution fridge</text><line x1="150" y1="150" x2="210" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="210" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="275.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">³He/⁴He mix</text><text x="275.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">phase boundary</text><line x1="340" y1="150" x2="400" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="400" y="120" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="470.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">~10 mK</text><text x="470.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">qubit stage</text></svg>

Superconducting quantum processors must be cooled to roughly 10 millikelvin — hundredths of a degree above absolute zero — to keep qubits coherent. The only practical way to reach and hold that temperature continuously is a dilution refrigerator, and dilution refrigerators run on helium-3.

The cooling exploits the physics of a helium-3/helium-4 mixture. Below about 0.87 K the mixture separates into a helium-3-rich phase and a dilute phase; forcing helium-3 across that phase boundary absorbs heat, much as evaporation cools a liquid. This provides continuous cooling power at millikelvin temperatures that no other technique matches in a practical package.
Every dilution fridge needs a helium-3 charge (tens of liters STP or more)
Larger quantum systems and more dilution units multiply demand
Global helium-3 supply is only a few kg/yr and largely allocated
Detection and defense uses compete for the same supply

At a ~1.97 kg/yr coproduct rate, a breeder foundry is a source on the scale of the entire existing market. That is why helium-3 offtake for quantum and cryogenic customers is part of Hyperion's product strategy. The point is strategic availability of a scarce enabling material, described here in physical terms only.

title: Helium-3 for Neutron Detection
lede: Helium-3 proportional counters are a workhorse neutron detector for security and science; the isotope's huge capture cross-section makes it ideal.
body: The detector of choice for neutrons

<svg viewBox="0 0 560 300" width="100%" style="max-width:560px;height:auto;display:block;margin:14px 0;font-family:var(--sans,sans-serif)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="20" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="85.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">neutron in</text><text x="85.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">thermal</text><line x1="150" y1="150" x2="210" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="210" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="275.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">³He(n,p)T</text><text x="275.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">charged products</text><line x1="340" y1="150" x2="400" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="400" y="120" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="470.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">charge pulse</text><text x="470.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">counted</text></svg>

Helium-3 is one of the best materials for detecting neutrons. It has a very large thermal-neutron capture cross-section through the reaction ³He(n,p)³H, which converts a neutron into a proton and a tritium nucleus. Those charged products ionize the gas and produce a clean, easily counted electrical pulse.

Packaged as a pressurized proportional counter, helium-3 detectors are efficient, gamma-insensitive, and stable, which is why they became the standard for radiation-portal monitors at borders and ports, for nuclear-material safeguards, and for neutron-scattering instruments in research.

When large-scale deployment of neutron portal monitors was undertaken for security, demand for helium-3 spiked far above the tritium-decay supply, causing a well-documented shortage. The episode showed that a single application can exhaust the world's helium-3 and drove a search for alternatives and for new supply.
³He counters remain preferred where performance matters most
Safeguards and security demand steady, assured supply
A breeder foundry adds new helium-3 at kg/yr scale
Detection-grade purity requirements are addressed in processing
Supplying detection-grade helium-3 is a strategic-availability argument, described in physical and supply terms only, with no commercial claim on this page.

lede: Global helium-3 supply is only a few kilograms per year from a shrinking source; a breeder coproduct near 1.97 kg/yr is significant against that scale.

Helium-3 is extraordinarily scarce on Earth. There is no ore, no atmospheric source of consequence, and no direct industrial synthesis. Essentially all terrestrial helium-3 comes from the decay of tritium, and the largest reservoir has been tritium produced decades ago for nuclear weapons, now decaying and being harvested.

That legacy source is finite and declining. Global availability has been on the order of a few to low tens of kilograms per year, and demand from neutron detection, quantum-computing cryogenics, and research has repeatedly strained it. The security-portal deployment of the 2000s caused an acute shortage that has shaped policy since.
Why a breeder changes the picture
Legacy weapons-tritium supply is shrinking, not growing
Quantum computing is a new, expanding demand source
No new large terrestrial source exists absent fusion breeding
A foundry at ~1.97 kg/yr adds supply on the scale of the market

Hyperion does not need to dominate energy markets to be strategically important; producing helium-3 at kilogram-per-year scale addresses a genuine, documented supply constraint on quantum and detection technologies. This is a materials-availability argument. It carries no commercial content by policy — only the physical fact of scarce supply and a new source for it.
The coproduct figure remains contingent on the tritium breeding and inventory gates being closed at FOAK and beyond.

title: Collecting Helium-3 from Decay
lede: Helium-3 is separated from stored tritium during routine processing; because it is inert and unabsorbed, it collects as a gas ready for purification.
body: <svg viewBox="0 0 560 300" width="100%" style="max-width:560px;height:auto;display:block;margin:14px 0;font-family:var(--sans,sans-serif)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="20" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="85.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Stored T</text><text x="85.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">decaying</text><line x1="150" y1="150" x2="210" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="210" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="275.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Separation</text><text x="275.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">He-3 off-gas</text><line x1="340" y1="150" x2="400" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="400" y="120" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="470.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Purified He-3</text><text x="470.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">product</text></svg>

Helium-3 collection is a separation task, not a production task — the atoms are already being made by decay inside the stored tritium. The job is to remove the accumulated helium-3 cleanly, both to harvest the product and to keep the tritium fuel pure.

This is comparatively straightforward because helium-3 is chemically inert and is not absorbed by the metal-hydride getter beds that store tritium. As tritium decays on a bed, helium-3 collects as a free gas in the headspace and can be pumped off. Any helium-3 mixed with tritium gas is separated by the isotope-separation system, exploiting the mass and chemical differences between inert helium and reactive hydrogen isotopes.
Tritium decays on getter beds and in the fuel loop
Inert He-3 accumulates as a non-absorbed gas
Periodic pump-off removes He-3 from storage headspace
Isotope separation strips He-3 from tritium gas streams
Collected He-3 is purified and assayed to grade

How much helium-3 is collected per year depends directly on how much tritium is held and for how long — the inventory-management choice. The ~1.97 kg/yr figure reflects the reference inventory. Collection efficiency and cadence, part of the design-and-simulation program, set how much of the decayed helium-3 is actually recovered as product.

title: Helium-3 Purity and Grades
lede: Quantum cryogenics and neutron detection demand very pure helium-3, free of residual tritium and helium-4; purification and assay set the product grade.
