Helium-3 harvested from tritium decay is not immediately product-grade. It can carry residual tritium (a radioactive contaminant), helium-4 (from any ⁴He present and from tritium handling), and trace impurities. Different applications set different purity requirements, so the foundry produces to a specification and assays each batch.

For quantum-computing dilution refrigerators, residual tritium is unacceptable: it is radioactive, and any tritium in the ³He/⁴He mixture contaminates a closed cryogenic system that customers expect to be clean. For neutron detectors, tritium background and impurities degrade counting performance. Purification to remove residual tritium and unwanted helium-4 is therefore essential.
Isotopic purity: fraction that is genuinely ³He vs ⁴He
Radiopurity: residual tritium below the required threshold
Chemical purity: freedom from moisture and other gases
Assay: mass spectrometry and gas analysis certify each batch

Because helium-3 comes from decayed tritium, its provenance and radiopurity must be documented for regulated uses. Assay and certification tie back to the tritium accountancy system, so a delivered batch carries a verified composition. Grade specifications are a design-and-process matter, described physically and with no commercial content on this page.
This page describes a design-and-simulation study, not a built machine. Construction begins Q2 2027; first-of-a-kind (FOAK) first tritium is targeted near 2030. No net-gain claim is made before FOAK.

D–T fusion neutrons are born at 14.1 MeV — several times more energetic than the ~1–2 MeV neutrons that dominate a fission reactor. That energy difference is not a detail; it changes which nuclear reactions occur and how materials are damaged, which is why a 14 MeV source is scientifically distinct.
Threshold reactions: (n,2n), (n,α), and (n,p) channels that only open above a few MeV
Helium and hydrogen production in materials via (n,α) and (n,p) — the cause of swelling and embrittlement unique to fusion
Higher displacement energy per collision, altering the damage cascade
Transmutation pathways relevant to activation and to isotope production

The most important of these for fusion engineering is helium production. Fast neutrons knock alpha particles out of structural atoms, and that helium collects at grain boundaries and voids, embrittling and swelling the material in ways fission-spectrum testing cannot reproduce. Predicting how a fusion first wall ages requires a fusion-energy neutron source that reaches these channels.

Fission reactors have the wrong spectrum. Accelerator and spallation sources approximate fusion conditions but with limited volume or fidelity. A running D–T machine at 85.0 MW provides genuine 14 MeV neutrons in usable quantity, which is why the flux itself is offered as a materials-qualification and activation service. This is a design-and-simulation capability until FOAK operates.

Fusion power plants will expose structural materials to intense 14 MeV neutron flux for years. Before any of those materials can be certified for service, they must be tested under representative irradiation — and until now there has been no dedicated facility providing fusion-energy neutrons in adequate quantity. Hyperion's flux is offered to fill that gap.

Test articles — candidate steels, tungsten and its alloys, silicon carbide composites, REBCO tape, ceramics, and joints — are placed in irradiation positions where they receive a known 14 MeV fluence. After irradiation they undergo post-irradiation examination: mechanical testing, microscopy, and measurement of swelling, embrittlement, and helium content.
A genuine 14 MeV spectrum, not a fission surrogate
Known, instrumented fluence and temperature conditions
Access positions for third-party and program test articles
Data to underpin materials qualification and licensing

Flux routed to irradiation ports is flux not available for breeding, so materials service competes with tritium production for the same neutron budget. The design balances dedicated test volume against blanket coverage. How much qualification flux can be offered while meeting breeding targets is a design-and-simulation allocation, firmed up as the machine is built.

Neutron damage to a solid is quantified primarily by displacements per atom (dpa): the average number of times each atom is knocked from its lattice site over an irradiation. A high-dpa material has been thoroughly rearranged at the atomic scale, which drives hardening, swelling, and loss of ductility.

But dpa alone does not capture fusion damage. The 14 MeV spectrum also produces helium inside the material through (n,α) reactions, and hydrogen through (n,p). The ratio of helium produced to displacements — the He/dpa ratio — is far higher for fusion neutrons than for fission neutrons, and it is this transmuted helium that most aggressively embrittles and swells fusion structures.
Same dpa, different He content → different real damage
Fission testing under-produces helium, understating embrittlement
Helium collects at grain boundaries and voids, causing swelling
Accurate lifetime prediction needs the correct He/dpa ratio

Because Hyperion delivers real 14 MeV neutrons, materials irradiated in it accumulate dpa and helium in the correct proportion for fusion service. That makes the resulting data directly usable for qualifying first-wall and blanket materials, where the center post and first wall themselves face limited lifetime — the center post is noted at roughly 0.01 fpy. Damage prediction remains a design-and-simulation subject validated by irradiation data at FOAK and beyond.

Irradiation testing is only as relevant as the neutron energy spectrum it uses. Two facilities can deliver the same total flux yet cause entirely different damage if their spectra differ, because reaction cross-sections and damage physics are energy-dependent. For qualifying fusion materials, the spectrum must resemble that of a D–T plant.
Fission reactors: spectrum peaks near 1–2 MeV; no 14 MeV component; wrong He/dpa
Spallation sources: broad high-energy tail, but different reaction mix and limited volume
Accelerator D–Li sources (e.g., IFMIF-class): fusion-like but not a burning plasma, limited volume
D–T fusion (Hyperion): genuine 14.1 MeV birth spectrum in bulk

The distinctive feature of the fusion spectrum is the sharp 14.1 MeV peak, which opens the threshold reactions responsible for helium and hydrogen generation. Softening or omitting that peak, as fission testing does, systematically misrepresents how a material will behave in a fusion plant.

Placing test articles inside a running D–T machine exposes them to the actual plant spectrum, including its spatial and temporal variation, rather than an approximation. Combined with controlled temperature and instrumented fluence, this yields qualification-grade data. Hyperion's ability to offer this at 85.0 MW is a design-and-simulation capability, validated once the machine operates at FOAK.

To turn raw flux into qualification data, Hyperion incorporates materials test stations: instrumented positions where test articles are held in the neutron field. Their placement sets the flux and spectrum each sample sees, so positions are characterized by neutronics before use.
Known neutron flux and spectrum at the sample position
Controlled and monitored temperature (damage is temperature-dependent)
Fluence dosimetry: foils and monitors that record the actual dose received
Access for insertion and retrieval without breaking the whole machine
Containment for any activated or tritiated samples

Temperature control matters because radiation damage anneals and evolves differently at different temperatures; a sample must be irradiated at its intended service temperature for the data to be meaningful. Dosimetry matters because a qualification claim requires the delivered dose to be measured, not assumed.

Every test position occupies solid angle that could otherwise hold blanket, so test-station volume trades directly against blanket coverage and TBR. The design allocates a bounded fraction of the neutron budget to services while protecting the breeding mission. The number and capability of stations is a design-and-simulation choice, finalized as the machine is engineered toward FOAK.

Beyond breeding tritium and testing materials, Hyperion's neutron flux can activate deliberately chosen target materials to produce specific radioisotopes. When a stable nucleus absorbs a neutron or undergoes an (n,2n), (n,p), or (n,α) reaction, it can transmute into a useful radioactive or stable isotope.

The 14 MeV spectrum is again distinctive: it opens threshold reaction channels unavailable to the thermal neutrons of a fission reactor, so a fusion source can reach isotopes and production routes that are difficult or impossible elsewhere. Targets are placed in dedicated irradiation positions, irradiated to a planned fluence, then removed and processed.
Isotopes reachable via fast/threshold reactions not favored in fission
Complement to the tritium and helium-3 streams

Activation draws on the same finite neutron budget as breeding and materials testing, so it is allocated deliberately. Activated targets are radioactive and enter the same accountancy and handling framework as the other products. The specific isotope menu is a design-and-simulation and licensing question; this page makes no economic or market claim, only the physical capability.

title: Medical Isotope Potential
lede: A 14 MeV source can reach production routes for certain medical and research isotopes — a potential service, stated cautiously and without economics.

The medical-isotope supply chain depends heavily on a small number of aging fission reactors, and shortages of key diagnostic and therapeutic isotopes have been a recurring problem. A fusion neutron source offers alternative production routes, particularly for isotopes best reached by fast or threshold reactions that fission spectra do not favor.

Kronos states this as a potential, not a committed product. Realizing medical-isotope production requires target chemistry, hot-cell processing, radiochemical purification, and stringent regulatory qualification for medical use — a substantial program beyond simply having neutrons. The physics capability is real; the pathway to certified medical product is long.
Why a fusion source is interesting here
Threshold (n,2n)/(n,p) routes can yield high-specific-activity products
Carrier-free production for some isotopes via specific reactions
Diversifies supply away from a fragile fission-reactor base

No medical isotope is claimed as a deliverable of Hyperion today. The machine is a design-and-simulation study, and any medical-isotope service would follow its own qualification and licensing path well after FOAK. This page describes physical potential only and makes no commercial claim of any kind.

title: Transmutation and Activation Products
lede: Neutrons transmute nuclei in fuel, structure, and targets; understanding these products matters for services, waste, and honest safety accounting.

Any material in a neutron field is transmuted to some degree: nuclei capture neutrons or undergo threshold reactions and become different nuclides. In Hyperion this happens deliberately (breeding tritium, activating chosen targets) and unavoidably (activation of structure, coolant, and the first wall). Both must be understood.
Tritium breeding: ⁶Li(n,α)³H — the primary product
Neutron multiplication: (n,2n) on Be or Pb
Target activation: chosen (n,x) routes for isotope services

Structural steel, tungsten, coolant, and the hafnium-carbide-protected first wall all activate under 14 MeV irradiation, producing radioactive nuclides with a range of half-lives. This activation is why components have handling and disposal requirements, and why the center post — with its limited lifetime near 0.01 fpy — is a scheduled replacement item. Accounting for activation products honestly is part of the safety and waste case, not a side note.
Why it belongs on a products page

What Hyperion makes includes intended products and unintended activation, and candor requires naming both. The neutronics that predict tritium yield are the same neutronics that predict component activation. Both are design-and-simulation results, confirmed by measurement once the machine runs at FOAK.

title: Neutron Fluence Planning
lede: Fluence — flux integrated over time — is the currency of irradiation; planning it lets breeding, testing, and services share a finite neutron budget.
body: <svg viewBox="0 0 560 300" width="100%" style="max-width:560px;height:auto;display:block;margin:14px 0;font-family:var(--sans,sans-serif)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="20" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="85.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Flux</text><text x="85.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">n/cm²/s</text><line x1="150" y1="150" x2="210" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="210" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="275.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">× exposure time</text><text x="275.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">campaign</text><line x1="340" y1="150" x2="400" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="400" y="120" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="470.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Fluence</text><text x="470.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">n/cm² delivered</text></svg>

Flux is the instantaneous rate of neutrons crossing a surface; fluence is that flux integrated over time — the total dose a sample or component accumulates. Nearly every irradiation outcome (dpa, helium production, activation, breeding) depends on fluence, so planning it is how the foundry manages what it makes.

Fluence planning allocates the finite neutron budget across missions and over the operating schedule. A materials test article needs a target dpa, which sets its required fluence and therefore its exposure time in a given flux position. A breeding campaign needs sustained fluence in the blanket. A target for activation needs a specific fluence to reach the desired isotope yield without over-activating.
Breeding fluence in the blanket (the primary mission)
Test-article fluence for materials qualification campaigns
Target fluence for activation and isotope services
Component fluence limits — e.g., center-post lifetime near 0.01 fpy
Machine availability and duty cycle over the campaign

Fluence also determines how long components last. The center post accumulates damage and must be replaced on a schedule set by its fluence limit. Planning therefore couples what the machine produces to when it must be maintained. All of this is a design-and-simulation projection, calibrated against measured dosimetry once Hyperion operates.

lede: Hyperion's products are offered as offtake: tritium as fusion feedstock, helium-3 for quantum and detection, and 14 MeV neutron services.

Because Hyperion is sized to a supply requirement rather than a power rating, its outputs are treated as offtake: material and services delivered to identified users. The three streams — tritium, helium-3, and 14 MeV neutron flux — serve different customers and follow different delivery and qualification paths.
Tritium: feedstock for D–T fusion programs, neutron targets, and internal fleet startup
Helium-3: dilution-refrigeration and detector customers in quantum computing, cryogenics, and security
14 MeV neutrons: irradiation and activation services for materials qualification and research

Each stream is coupled to the same neutron budget, so offtake planning is inseparable from the breeding trade. Tritium and helium-3 are physical shipments requiring accountancy, containment, and radiopurity certification; neutron services are delivered in-machine as irradiation positions and campaigns.
What offtake does not include here

This overview describes what is supplied and to whom, in physical and strategic terms. Consistent with Kronos policy, it makes no statement about commercial terms of any kind. Offtake here means the material and service streams themselves — their nature, users, and dependencies.

All offtake volumes depend on the breeding and self-sufficiency gates. The tritium and helium-3 figures are design targets contingent on net TBR at the 1.8 point; neutron-service capacity depends on how the budget is allocated. These are design-and-simulation commitments until FOAK demonstrates production.
This page describes a design-and-simulation study, not a built machine. Construction begins Q2 2027; first-of-a-kind (FOAK) first tritium is targeted near 2030. No net-gain claim is made before FOAK.

lede: Surplus tritium above self-sufficiency can be supplied to fusion programs and neutron-target users — the offtake that also seeds new units.

Tritium offtake is the surplus tritium remaining after the machine covers its own fuel needs, losses, and startup reserves. Because there is no natural tritium reservoir and only limited fission-derived supply, any assured new source of tritium is strategically important to the entire D–T fusion field.
D–T fusion experiments and prototypes that do not breed their own
Internal Kronos fleet startup — charging the next unit
Research and calibration users of tritium

Deliveries are physical shipments of a controlled radioactive material. Each batch is purified, separated from accumulated helium-3, assayed by calorimetry and gas analysis, and documented under the tritium accountancy system. Containment, transport authorization, and radiopurity certification accompany every shipment.
The surplus is set by breeding

Only tritium bred above self-sufficiency is available as external offtake, so the volume is governed directly by net TBR. At a thin net margin, little is available; at the reference 1.8 target, the ~4 kg/yr class supports meaningful offtake and fleet seeding. Because the net-TBR reconciliation is open, offtake volumes are design targets, not committed quantities, before FOAK.
This page addresses the material stream and its users only, with no commercial terms stated, per policy.

Helium-3 offtake is the purified helium-3 harvested from decaying tritium and delivered to users for whom it is an enabling material. At a coproduct rate near 1.97 kg/yr, the foundry contributes supply on the scale of the entire existing global market for the isotope.
Quantum computing: dilution refrigerators cooling superconducting processors
Neutron detection: ³He proportional counters for security and safeguards
Specialized research and, potentially, hyperpolarized ³He medical imaging

Each customer class has purity and documentation requirements. Quantum and cryogenic users need radiopure helium-3 free of residual tritium; detection users need consistent isotopic and chemical purity. The product is assayed and certified to grade, with provenance traceable to the tritium accountancy system because the helium-3 originates from decayed tritium.

Because helium-3 grows from held tritium, offtake volume depends on inventory-management choices as well as breeding. Holding tritium longer yields more helium-3 but consumes tritium to decay; the balance between tritium and helium-3 offtake is a deliberate operating decision.

This is a strategic-availability statement about a scarce material and its users, with no commercial claim, consistent with Kronos policy. Volumes remain design targets contingent on the breeding and inventory gates until FOAK.

Not every product leaves the machine as a shipped isotope. The 14 MeV neutron flux itself is offered as a service: users place test articles or activation targets in instrumented irradiation positions and receive a controlled, documented dose. This is neutron-services offtake.
Materials qualification: irradiate structural and functional materials to target dpa/fluence, then return them for post-irradiation examination
Activation: irradiate chosen targets to transmute them into research or feedstock isotopes

Both are delivered as campaigns with defined flux positions, target fluence, controlled temperature, and dosimetry so the delivered dose is measured rather than assumed. Activated and tritiated samples are handled under the same accountancy and containment framework as the shipped isotope products.

Service flux competes directly with breeding for the finite neutron budget, so the machine allocates a bounded fraction to services while protecting the tritium mission. The available service volume is therefore a design-and-simulation allocation, finalized as the machine is engineered and confirmed once it operates at FOAK.

There is no other running D–T source offering genuine 14 MeV irradiation in usable quantity, which is what makes this service distinctive for fusion materials qualification. This page describes the service and its users only, with no commercial terms stated, per policy.

title: Products, Not Power
lede: Hyperion is judged by what it makes, not by net electricity; the breeder needs fusion gain, not net-electric output, to deliver its products.
body: <svg viewBox="0 0 560 300" width="100%" style="max-width:560px;height:auto;display:block;margin:14px 0;font-family:var(--sans,sans-serif)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="20" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="85.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Fusion gain</text><text x="85.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">Q_sci 3.076</text><line x1="150" y1="150" x2="210" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="210" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="275.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Neutron flux</text><text x="275.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">85.0 MW fusion</text><line x1="340" y1="150" x2="400" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="400" y="120" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="470.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Products</text><text x="470.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">T, He-3, n</text></svg>

Most fusion programs are judged by whether they can put net electricity on a grid. Hyperion is not. Its success criterion is production of tritium, helium-3, and 14 MeV neutrons — outputs that require fusion gain and a strong neutron source, but not net-electric output.

This distinction is fundamental. Net electricity requires that gross electrical output exceed all recirculating power for magnets, heating, cryogenics, and balance of plant — a harder threshold than scientific gain. Hyperion at Q_sci 3.076 and 85.0 MW makes the neutrons that drive its products without needing to cross the net-electric line. The neutron flux is the product.
Q_sci 3.076 is a gain figure, not a net-electric claim
No net-gain or net-power claim is made before FOAK
The machine is sized to a supply requirement, not a MW target
Value is delivered as material and services, measured by assay

Net-electric output is the burner's (Aegis / MetroVolt) objective, pursued through direct energy conversion and gated on its own separate physics. The breeder deliberately does not depend on that harder demonstration. Keeping the two roles distinct is what lets the breeder deliver products first while the burner physics mature. This is a design-and-simulation study; construction begins Q2 2027.

Hyperion's product figures — the ~4 kg/yr tritium class, the ~1.97 kg/yr helium-3 coproduct, and the neutron-service capacity — are design-and-simulation targets, not demonstrated yields. Candor requires naming the gates each one depends on. These are physics-and-engineering findings, stated plainly to build trust, and none of them is an economic statement.
Local vs net TBR: a local breeding ratio of 1.8 is not the net as-built value once ports, gaps, structure, coolant, and holdup are included. The reconciliation at the 1.8 target is unresolved.
Tritium self-sufficiency: whether the machine breeds enough to fuel itself with surplus is not yet proven, and gates on net TBR clearing 1.0 with margin.
Center-post lifetime: the inboard center post has a limited life, noted near 0.01 fpy, which constrains availability and campaign planning.
Losses and holdup: the gap between bred and recoverable tritium must be bounded to keep the surplus real.

Closure comes from full-geometry neutronics, blanket and extraction engineering, and ultimately from measured tritium and helium-3 production at first-of-a-kind first tritium near 2030, with NOAK and BOAK refining the record. No net-gain claim is made before FOAK.

Overstated breeding claims are the most common failure point in fusion fuel-cycle proposals. By stating TBR as a lever, separating local from net, and naming self-sufficiency and center-post lifetime as open, Kronos keeps the product story defensible. The figures are honest targets; the gates are the conditions under which they become facts.

title: Isotope Assay and Quality
lede: Before any product ships, it is assayed and certified: tritium by calorimetry and gas analysis, helium-3 for isotopic and radiopurity grade.
body: <svg viewBox="0 0 560 300" width="100%" style="max-width:560px;height:auto;display:block;margin:14px 0;font-family:var(--sans,sans-serif)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="20" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="85.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Product batch</text><text x="85.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">T or He-3</text><line x1="150" y1="150" x2="210" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="210" y="120" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="275.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Assay</text><text x="275.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">calorimetry / MS</text><line x1="340" y1="150" x2="400" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="400" y="120" width="140" height="60" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="470.0" y="147.0" fill="#F4E9CE" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Certified</text><text x="470.0" y="164.0" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">graded & documented</text></svg>

A foundry's credibility rests on delivering exactly what it says it delivers. Every batch of tritium and helium-3 is assayed and certified before it leaves, so product figures are backed by measurement rather than by the design model. Assay is also the link between what the machine makes and the accountancy system that tracks it.
Calorimetry: measuring the decay heat gives an accurate tritium mass
Gas analysis / mass spectrometry: composition and isotopic content
Helium-3 content: quantifies decay-accumulated daughter to be separated
Chemical purity: moisture and impurity levels

Helium-3 is certified for isotopic purity (³He vs ⁴He), radiopurity (residual tritium below the required threshold for quantum and cryogenic use), and chemical purity. Grade determines suitability: dilution-refrigeration customers require the strictest radiopurity, while some detection uses tolerate more. Each batch carries a certificate traceable to its tritium provenance.

Assay is what turns a design-and-simulation target into a verified quantity. The ~4 kg/yr class and ~1.97 kg/yr coproduct become real numbers only when assayed product accumulates from FOAK onward. Until then they are honest projections; assay is the discipline that will confirm or correct them. Assay carries no economic content — it certifies physical quantity and quality only.

lede: The spherical tokamak's inboard center post takes space that cannot breed and must be shielded; this geometry directly limits inboard TBR.
body: The cost of a compact machine

Hyperion is a spherical tokamak with aspect ratio A 2.5 and major radius R0 1.2 m, which makes it compact and efficient but places a slim center post on the inboard side carrying the toroidal-field conductors up to a peak field of 16.84 T. That center post is central to why the machine works — and a real constraint on breeding.

Inboard space occupied by the center post and its shielding is space that cannot hold a full breeding blanket. Because inboard coverage contributes significantly to TBR, this geometry caps how much can be bred there. The trade is fundamental to the spherical-tokamak choice, not a flaw to be engineered away.
Breeding: reduced inboard blanket lowers achievable net TBR
Shielding: the center post must be protected from neutron damage
Lifetime: even shielded, the center post has a limited life near 0.01 fpy
Both compete for the same scarce inboard volume

The response is to maximize outboard and top/bottom breeding, use neutron multiplication to recover budget, and accept scheduled center-post replacement. Whether the resulting net TBR meets the 1.8 target is precisely the open reconciliation. The trade is a design-and-simulation subject, and the center-post lifetime is stated candidly as a constraint on availability and on what the machine can make over time.

title: The Foundry's Role in the Fleet
lede: Hyperion is the fuel source for the wider program: it seeds new breeders and supplies the tritium and helium-3 the burner pathway will need.
body: The machine the rest depends on

The breeder (Hyperion) is built first because everything else depends on what it makes. Its products are not just external offtake; they are the fuel that lets the program grow. This is the foundry's role in the FOAK → NOAK → BOAK path and in the eventual burner fuel cycle.
Seed new breeders: surplus tritium above self-sufficiency charges the next unit's startup inventory
Supply the field: external tritium offtake to programs without their own breeding
Feed the burner pathway: helium-3 coproduct is the fuel the D–3He burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) will eventually consume

The link to the burner is direct. The burner runs on deuterium and helium-3, and helium-3 has no terrestrial source except tritium decay. A breeder foundry is therefore the natural first supplier of burner fuel, alongside the lunar helium-3 pathway envisioned for fleet-scale burner operation.

Because the foundry's products enable both fleet growth and the burner, building it first is a logical consequence of what it makes, not merely a schedule choice. Net TBR governs how fast this can proceed: higher breeding means faster seeding and more offtake. All of it is contingent on the self-sufficiency gate and remains a design-and-simulation plan; construction begins Q2 2027.
